issues.claim: The ruling caps damages at one recovery per person per statutory subsection
issues.issue: The phrase 'per statutory subsection' is an imprecise simplification. The actual amendment language (Public Act 103-0769) limits recovery for violations of Sections 15(b) and 15(d) involving 'the same biometric identifier or biometric information from the same person using the same method of collection.' The 'per statutory subsection' framing omits the 'same method of collection' and 'same biometric identifier' qualifiers, which could matter in cases involving multiple biometric types or collection methods.
issues.suggested_fix: Revise to: 'caps damages at one recovery per person for each type of violation involving the same biometric identifier collected using the same method' or simply 'caps damages at one recovery per person per type of violation' with a parenthetical noting the method-of-collection qualifier.

issues.claim: The court distinguished the Cothron per-scan accrual rule as addressing statute-of-limitations timing under Section 15
issues.issue: Characterizing Cothron as addressing 'statute-of-limitations timing' is a simplification. Cothron's holding was about claim accrual — specifically, that a separate claim accrues each time a biometric identifier is scanned or transmitted in violation of Sections 15(b) and 15(d). While accrual has statute-of-limitations implications (it determines when the limitations clock starts), the primary holding was about when separate violations arise, not statute-of-limitations timing per se. The Clay court distinguished accrual (Section 15) from damages calculation (Section 20), which is accurately captured, but the 'statute-of-limitations timing' characterization slightly misrepresents Cothron's focus.
issues.suggested_fix: Revise to: 'The court distinguished the Cothron per-scan accrual rule as addressing when separate violations arise under Section 15, not the separate question of damages calculation under Section 20.'
